The fog horn of the *Aethelgard* did not scream; it groaned. It was a low, tectonic rumble that vibrated through the soles of Elias Thorne’s boots, traveling up his spine and settling in the marrow of his bones. He stood at the base of the spiral staircase, the iron rungs cold and slick with the condensation that clung to every surface of the lighthouse.

Elias was Lighthouse Keeper #0.

The title was not one he had chosen, nor was it one that appeared in any official maritime registry. The Coast Guard logs listed him as "Unassigned Personnel," a bureaucratic ghost who had signed a contract with a government agency that no longer existed, in a port that had been submerged by rising sea levels three decades prior. He lived in the only structure on the island that the tides had not yet claimed, a lighthouse that seemed to defy the physics of the surrounding ocean. The island itself was a jagged tooth of black basalt, barely a quarter-mile wide, rising from the churning grey water of the North Atlantic.

For forty years, Elias had kept the light.

It was not a simple job. The light was not a beam of electricity. It was a beam of memory.

Elias climbed. One hundred and twelve steps. He had counted them so many times that the number was etched into his muscle memory. At the top, the lantern room was a glass eye staring out into the void. The mechanism inside was a complex array of prisms and lenses, but the source of the light was a small, glass orb sitting in the center of the ba

The story of Lighthouse Keeper #0 is not one of romance, nor is it a tale of survival against the elements. It is a story of geometry, of the weight of light, and of the terrible, quiet burden of being the first.

To understand Keeper #0, one must first understand the architecture of the world. Most people believe the lighthouses are scattered randomly along the jagged teeth of the coastline, standing guard against the dark. They are wrong. The lighthouses are a chain. A rigid, unbroken chain that stretches from the mouth of the world to its edge. If one link fails, the whole structure collapses. The light at the end of the chain is not meant to guide ships in; it is meant to mark the boundary of the known. Beyond the light, there is nothing. There is only the Void.

Keeper #0 lived at the beginning of the chain. His station was not on a cliff or an island, but on a pillar of black basalt that rose from the ocean floor, three miles off the coast of the mainland. It was a solitary rock, slick with algae and barnacles, accessible only by a submersible that arrived once every six months. The lighthouse itself was a structure of white concrete and glass, stark against the grey churning water. It had no room for a garden, no porch for a cat, and no window that faced the land. Every window faced the sea. Every shadow fell toward the horizon.

His name was Elias. But in the logs, he was simply listed as Keeper #0. The number was not a rank; it was a coordinate. He was the zero point
